title: US Expands Social Media Vetting to Media and USMCA Visas From Oct 1
excerpt: Starting October 1, applicants for I, TN, and TD visas must set all social media profiles to public, as the State Department extends its online-presence review to three more nonimmigrant visa categories.
body:
• The State Department will expand its online-presence review to I (foreign media), TN (USMCA professionals), and TD (their dependents) visa applicants, effective October 1, 2026.
  • Applicants in these categories are instructed to set the privacy settings on all social media profiles to "public" or "open" before their visa interviews.
  • Indian journalists working for recognized foreign media organizations can be directly affected under the I-visa expansion; TN visas are limited to citizens of Canada and Mexico.
  • The expansion adds to a growing list of vetted categories that already includes students, H-1B workers, exchange visitors, fiancé(e)s, and religious workers.

The U.S. Department of State will expand its social media vetting program to three more nonimmigrant visa categories beginning October 1, 2026, requiring applicants for I, TN, and TD visas to open their online profiles to consular scrutiny.

The announcement, documented by the American Immigration Lawyers Association as AILA Doc. No. 26091803 on September 18, 2026, adds foreign media representatives (I), USMCA professionals (TN), and the dependents of TN holders (TD) to the growing roster of visa applicants subject to what the State Department calls an "online presence review." To support the enhanced vetting, applicants in these categories are instructed to set the privacy settings on all of their social media profiles to "public" or "open."

A steady expansion of digital vetting

The policy did not arrive out of nowhere. The State Department's online presence review already covers a wide swath of nonimmigrant categories: students (F-1, F-2, M-1, M-2), temporary workers and their dependents (H-1B, H-3, H-4), exchange visitors (J-1, J-2), fiancé(e)s (K-1, K-2, K-3), religious workers (R-1, R-2), international cultural exchange participants (Q), and diplomatic and official categories (A-3, C-3, G-5), among others.

The groundwork for mandatory public profiles was laid in June 2025, when the State Department told all F, M, and J visa applicants to make their social media accounts public to facilitate vetting of identity and admissibility. That came after a temporary suspension of student visa interviews in May 2025 while the government prepared the expanded screening apparatus. Since 2019, visa applicants have been required to disclose their social media identifiers on application forms; the newer policy goes further by demanding public access to the content itself.

"Visa adjudications are national security decisions. U.S. visas remain a discretionary benefit rather than an entitlement."

— U.S. Department of State, per its visa screening announcement

What the new categories cover

The I visa covers representatives of foreign media — journalists, film crews, and others working for press, radio, film, or print organizations who are traveling temporarily to the United States to pursue their profession. TN status is a NAFTA-successor USMCA benefit available to professionals from Canada and Mexico, and TD status covers their spouses and unmarried children under 21.

With the October 1 additions, the State Department is continuing what immigration firm Envoy Global describes as a steady broadening of the heightened online presence review during adjudication. The firm cautions employers and foreign nationals to watch for emerging trends, such as 221(g) administrative processing requests tied to social media reviews.

"The Department of State relies on all available sources of information during visa screening and vetting to identify applicants who may be inadmissible to the U.S., including individuals who may pose a threat to national security or public safety."

— U.S. Department of State

What it means for Indian applicants

For the Indian diaspora, the most direct effect is on journalists: Indian citizens working for recognized foreign media organizations are eligible for I visas for professional assignments in the United States, and they will now need to keep their social media profiles public through the adjudication process.

TN visas, by contrast, are restricted exclusively to citizens of Canada and Mexico, so Indian nationals cannot apply for TN status themselves. They can, however, qualify for TD visas as the spouse or unmarried child (under 21) of a valid TN holder, regardless of nationality — a pathway that could matter for Indian family members of Canadian or Mexican professionals.

For the large Indian cohort on H-1B visas, the policy is a reminder of the status quo: H-1B, H-3, and H-4 applicants are already subject to social media vetting.

What's next

Applicants in the newly covered categories should set their social media profiles to "public" or "open" now, and review their online presence for consistency with their stated purpose of travel. Immigration lawyers are watching whether the public-profiles requirement becomes the default for all nonimmigrant applicants.

The State Department's position is unambiguous: applicants must establish eligibility for the requested visa and demonstrate intent to comply with the terms of admission, and the agency continues to frame every visa decision as a national security decision.
image_caption: A U.S. passport sits beside a U.S. visa foil bearing entry stamps. The State Department will expand its social media vetting program to I, TN, and TD visa applicants effective October 1, 2026.
nri_angle: Indian journalists on I visas face the new public-profiles requirement, while Indians can obtain TD visas as dependents of TN holders; H-1B workers are already under social media vetting.
